verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that godwariness prepares the Prophet for the command not to obey the faithless and hypocrites. Their being joined in the prohibition indicates that the faithless sought something displeasing to God and the hypocrites supported them. God had wisely decided against this request and revealed His ruling, although carrying it out appears difficult without divine help; the Prophet is therefore directed to follow revelation and rely on God alone.

This reading supports reports on the occasion of revelation which say that, after Uḥud, Quraysh leaders entered Medina under the Prophet’s guarantee of safety and proposed mutual non-interference: he should leave them and their gods, and they would leave him and his God. The verse was then revealed, and he did not accept. This also explains the closing words, “Indeed Allah is all-knowing, all-wise,” and the following commands.
verses.2: Al-Mizan holds that, although the verse is general when read alone, its context makes it a command to follow and implement the revelation concerning the request of the disbelievers and hypocrites. “Indeed Allah is well aware of what you do” confirms this practical injunction.
verses.3: Al-Mizan explains that the command is general in isolation, but in its context directs the Prophet to trust God in carrying out revelation’s commands. The task is apparently too difficult to accomplish by ordinary means and naturally causes anxiety unless one relies on God, the means that no other means can overcome.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan takes the statement that God has not placed two hearts within a man to allude to the impossibility of simultaneously assenting to contradictory propositions: this would require two hearts, souls, or minds, whereas a person has only one. “Within” adds emphasis.

One interpretation makes this the rationale for abolishing ẓihār and adoption: a wife cannot at once be a man’s wife and mother, nor can another man’s son truly be his own son. Another plausible interpretation relates it to the preceding commands: obedience and loyalty to God cannot coexist in one heart with obedience and loyalty to the faithless and hypocrites, just as tawḥīd and shirk cannot coexist.

Ẓihār was the pre-Islamic divorce formula by which a man likened his wife’s back to his mother’s back. Islam abolished it: God has not legislatively made a wife repudiated through ẓihār into her husband’s mother, so the utterance has no legal effect. Likewise, adʿiyāʾ, children claimed as one’s own, are not actual sons and do not receive the legal status of natural sons, such as in inheritance and consanguinity; this practice too was abolished.

“That is a mere utterance of your mouths” may refer to both ẓihār and adoption, though its apparent reference is adoption, as the next verse concerns adoption. Attributing an adopted child to oneself has no basis in reality and thus no effect. In contrast, God’s speech corresponds to reality, and His legislation has real consequences and produces genuine benefit (maṣlaḥah). His guidance carries those whom He guides along the way of truth, goodness, and happiness; the verse thus intimates that people should abandon their own utterances and adhere to God’s word.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that the lām in li-ābāʾihim is exclusive: adopted children are to be called after, and attributed only to, their fathers. Such attribution is more just (aqsaṭ) with God. If their fathers are not personally known, they must not be attributed to anyone else, but called brethren in faith and kinsmen.

There is no sin in mistakenly calling them after someone other than their fathers through inattentiveness (sahw) or forgetfulness (nisyān). Deliberately doing so, however, is sinful. God’s being all-forgiving and all-merciful concerns such mistakes.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains that the faithful themselves are meant by “their own selves,” and that the Prophet’s being more entitled (awlā) to them means that he takes priority over them when there is a choice. Their protectiveness, loyalty, affection, generosity, and inclination are owed to him more than to themselves. They must protect him even by self-sacrifice, esteem and love him above themselves, and prefer his wish when it conflicts with their own. Because the expression is categorical (muṭlaq), this priority extends to worldly as well as religious matters.

The commentary rejects the view that the verse concerns only obedience to the Prophet’s summons, since that would add nothing beyond commands to obey the Messenger. It likewise rejects the interpretation that merely makes his relation to believers superior to their relation among themselves; this is not supported by the verse’s tenor.

The Prophet’s wives are their mothers by a legislative enactment (jaʿl tashrīʿī): they are owed maternal respect and may not be married after him. They do not, however, receive every legal consequence of actual motherhood: they do not inherit from the faithful, looking at their faces is not thereby permitted, and their daughters are not prohibited in marriage through consanguinity.

Ūlū al-arḥām means blood relations, “people of wombs,” and their priority over the faithful and Emigrants concerns inheritance. The Book of Allah may mean the Guarded Tablet, the Qur’an, or this sūrah. The verse abrogates the earlier inheritance of believers through emigration and religious brotherhood. It may also be read to say that the blood relatives of the faithful and Emigrants are more entitled to one another.

The exception, “barring any favour you may do your comrades,” is discontinuous: it refers to a testamentary bequest (waṣiyyah), not inheritance, and divine law limits it to one third of the estate. Its ruling too is written in the Guarded Tablet, the Qur’an, or the sūrah.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan states that the mīthāq belongs specifically to the Prophets as Prophets and is therefore distinct from the pledge taken from all humanity. Although this verse does not specify its terms, (3:81) indicates that it bound them to remain united in the message of religion and not differ over it.

All Prophets are first included, then the Prophet, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus son of Mary are singled out for special distinction. These are the Prophets endowed with resoluteness (ūlū ʿazm), who brought new codes and scriptures. Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus are listed in historical order, while the Prophet is named first despite coming last because of his superiority and nobility over them all. Calling it a harsh pledge (mīthāq ghalīẓ) emphasizes its strength.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan connects “So that He may question the truthful concerning their truthfulness” to the taking of the Prophets’ pledge: God took it so that He might question the truthful, while He has prepared a painful punishment for the faithless. Since the verse does not say that punishment was the purpose of the pledge, punishment results from the faithless people’s own faults rather than being its ultimate aim.

The commentary rejects readings that make the truthful the Prophets questioned on the Day of Resurrection about their nations, or that make the questioning concern their statements about God’s unity, justice, and religion, the conformity of speech and action, or their motives for truthfulness. The phrasing is instead like asking the wealthy about their wealth or the learned about their knowledge: it asks them to display what they possess. Thus the truthful are asked to manifest in speech and action the truthfulness within their hearts, namely through good deeds in this world.

This questioning justifies the moral duties arising from their pledge, by requiring them to make their inward truthfulness evident. Because this occurs in this world, the pledge to the Prophets must have been taken at a stage preceding worldly existence, the “realm of pre-existence,” as indicated by (7:172). These verses therefore point to a world before this one in which the mīthāq was taken; whoever is faithful to it displays that faithfulness here.

Although the pledge under discussion is the Prophets’ pledge, the faithless are mentioned generally: the Prophets were bound to unity in their teaching so that truthful persons might fulfil their duties, be guided, and manifest truthfulness in belief and practice, thereby earning reward, whereas the faithless face painful punishment. The shift from “We took” to “He may question” is also significant. The pledge to worship God alone without associating partners was taken through the angels, hence “We,” but God alone questions the truthful and prepares punishment, so that He alone may be worshipped.
verses.9: Al-Mizan says that this verse recalls God’s blessing upon the faithful during the Battle of Khandaq, when He protected them from a great coalition of polytheist forces drawn from tribes including the Ghaṭfān, Quraysh, Abyssinians, Kinānah, Banū Qurayẓah, and Banū al-Naḍīr. Though they besieged the believers from every side, God sent against them the freezing winter-night wind of al-Ṣabā and unseen angels to humiliate them. “When” either qualifies the blessing or indicates its permanence, while the sending of the wind and angels explains the blessing that followed the coalition’s arrival.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains that those approaching Medina from above, on its eastern side, were the Ghaṭfān, Banū Qurayẓah, and Banū al-Naḍīr; those coming from below, on its western side, were Quraysh with Kinānah and the Abyssinians. These descriptions further explain the coming of the hosts. The rolling eyes and hearts rising to throats portray terror like that of people at death. The misgivings belonged to the hypocrites and those with sick hearts, who expected the disbelievers to seize Medina, Islam to be destroyed and the Age of Ignorance restored, and claimed that God had deceived the faithful and their Prophet.
verses.11: Al-Mizan takes “there” to mean the time when the armies reached Medina. At that intensely difficult time, the faithful were tested and shaken by extreme terror. Here, “afflicted” means tested and “jolted” means agitated; shadīd denotes severity perceptible to the senses, unlike qawī, power not so perceived.
verses.12: Al-Mizan distinguishes those “in whose hearts is a sickness,” who are believers weak in faith, from hypocrites, who profess faith outwardly while concealing disbelief and call the Prophet God’s Messenger only for appearance’s sake. Ghurūr is to lead someone toward evil while presenting it as good. The promise they call delusion is Islam’s eventual victory over every religion; thus they reject God’s and His Messenger’s promise amid their present insecurity.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains that Yathrib was Medina’s former name, and muqām means a place of residence. Some urged the people to leave because remaining to confront the polytheist armies was futile. Others among the hypocrites and weak believers sought the Prophet’s permission to return, falsely claiming that their homes were exposed to thieves or enemy attack; their real purpose was flight.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains that the houses would have been invaded from their flanks, while the people in question are the hypocrites and those with sickness in their hearts. Fitnah here means apostasy: had the polytheist forces entered their homes and demanded that they renounce faith, they would have complied with scarcely any hesitation. Their adherence therefore lasts only while religion is easy; hardship makes them ready to abandon it immediately.
verses.15: Al-Mizan explains that their pledge not to turn their backs was a pledge not to flee battle. It may refer to their bayʿah to believe in God, His Messenger, and all that the Messenger brought, including jihād, from which flight is forbidden. Such pledges to God are accountable.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains that every soul dies at its appointed time, neither earlier nor later, so flight from death or killing cannot alter it. Even if fleeing could provide additional life, that enjoyment would be only brief and would inevitably end.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says that, just as flight cannot avert an appointed death, no one can prevent the good or harm that God wills, nor protect a person from it. One should therefore entrust the matter to God, steadfastly obey His commands, and rely upon Him. Because those with sick hearts are preoccupied by concealed faithlessness, the address shifts from commanding the Prophet to speak to them to directly declaring that they will find no protector or helper besides Allah.
verses.18: Al-Mizan identifies those who hinder others from joining the Prophet and fighting as hypocrites. They summon fellow hypocrites or weak believers away from battle and participate only slightly, miserly with themselves. When danger comes, they stare in deathlike terror; once it passes, they lash the believers with sharp speech while begrudging them their gains. Their pretence does not make faith take root in their hearts, so God renders their deeds futile, which is easy for Him.
verses.19: Al-Mizan identifies those who hinder others from joining the Prophet and fighting as hypocrites. They summon fellow hypocrites or weak believers away from battle and participate only slightly, miserly with themselves. When danger comes, they stare in deathlike terror; once it passes, they lash the believers with sharp speech while begrudging them their gains. Their pretence does not make faith take root in their hearts, so God renders their deeds futile, which is easy for Him.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that their terror is so intense that they imagine the confederates have not departed. If the confederates returned, they would wish to be outside Medina in the desert among the Bedouins, merely asking about events there. Even if they remained with the believers, they would contribute little fighting, since they mostly avoid battle.
verses.21: Al-Mizan explains that the Messenger himself is a good exemplar to be imitated, and that the verse expresses an abiding duty of the faithful to follow him in words and deeds. They see him suffer for God’s sake, remain present on the battlefield, and exert himself fully in God’s cause. It prefers reading the verse as saying that he is in himself the exemplar, rather than merely that he possesses an imitable quality. This imitation belongs not to everyone called a believer, but to those of true faith whose hearts are devoted to God and the Last Day, who act righteously and remember God abundantly; such people do not forget their Lord and follow the Prophet’s conduct.
verses.22: Al-Mizan says that, when the sincere faithful saw the confederate armies besieging Medina, the event increased their guidance, insight, faith, and submission, unlike the doubts of the hypocrites and weak believers. “This is what Allah and His Messenger had promised us” refers to what they saw before them. Some interpret the promise as the Prophet’s foretelling of the confederates’ coming; others as the promise that the faithful would undergo the severe trials suffered by earlier prophets and believers, followed by God’s help. Both interpretations can be correct because the promise is ascribed jointly to Allah and His Messenger. Their testimony to its truth increased their faith in God and His Messenger and their submission to the command to support God’s religion and strive in His way.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains naḥb as an obligatory vow whose fulfilment is payment in full. The faithful prove the truth of their pledge by standing firm before the enemy, in contrast with those who pledged not to flee but failed. Those who have fulfilled their pledge are those who have died or been killed in God’s way; those who still wait await that end. Neither group has changed at all from its original pledge and promise.
verses.24: Al-Mizan explains the verse as the purpose behind the preceding accounts of faithful and hypocrites: God rewards the faithful who have been true to their pledges because of that truthfulness, while He may punish the hypocrites if they do not repent, or accept their repentance and forgive them if they do. His forgiveness and mercy also show how sin may become a step toward forgiveness and happiness—not as sin itself, but when it awakens shame, repentance, and liberation from wrongdoing.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains that God sent the faithless back in ghayẓ, a state combining fury and distress, without the “good” they sought—victory over the Prophet and the faithful. He spared the faithful the need to fight, and this manifests His irresistible strength and might.
verses.26: Al-Mizan identifies those among the People of the Book who supported the polytheists as the Jewish Banū Qurayẓah. They were brought down from their fortified strongholds—perhaps “brought down” is used because the fortifications stood high above their enemies—while terror was cast into their hearts. The men were killed, and the women and children taken captive. God then gave the believers their land, houses, and possessions, as well as land they had not trodden: either Khaybar or booty-land not disturbed by horses or mounts. Interpretations extending this to every future conquest, Mecca, or the lands of the Romans and Persians do not accord with the verses’ tone and context. Allah has power over all things.
verses.27: Al-Mizan identifies those among the People of the Book who supported the polytheists as the Jewish Banū Qurayẓah. They were brought down from their fortified strongholds—perhaps “brought down” is used because the fortifications stood high above their enemies—while terror was cast into their hearts. The men were killed, and the women and children taken captive. God then gave the believers their land, houses, and possessions, as well as land they had not trodden: either Khaybar or booty-land not disturbed by horses or mounts. Interpretations extending this to every future conquest, Mecca, or the lands of the Romans and Persians do not accord with the verses’ tone and context. Allah has power over all things.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan understands these verses to have been revealed because the Prophet’s wives, or some of them, suffered poverty and need in his household and complained of their circumstances. God therefore commanded the Prophet to offer them a choice: they could leave him, receive a financial settlement, and seek the worldly comfort they wanted; or they could remain with him in hardship, choosing Allah, His Messenger, and the hereafter.

The two choices are mutually opposed. To desire the worldly life and its ornaments is to attach one’s heart firmly to them, even if one also claims to desire the hereafter; to desire the hereafter is to make it one’s heartfelt priority, whether or not one happens to enjoy some worldly ease. Thus, they could not combine a life of luxury, finery, and amusement in the Prophet’s house with the choice of the hereafter. If they chose the world, the Prophet was required to divorce them and give them wealth; if they chose Allah, His Messenger, and the eternal abode, they had to remain married to him and patiently bear their restricted circumstances.

The promised great reward was not automatic by virtue of marriage to the Prophet. It depended additionally on their acting righteously and virtuously; otherwise, they would lose both this world and the next. Marriage to the Prophet confers honour only when joined with righteousness and reverence, for honour before God rests not on kinship, nobility, or ancestry but on reverence.

The commentary explains that taʿālayna, “come,” means to present their choice, not literally to move toward the Prophet. Umattiʿkunna means that he would give them a sum of wealth upon divorce; usarriḥkunna means divorce; and sarāḥan jamīlan means an amicable separation without conflict or ill-feeling. Although some exegetes derive general legal rulings from these verses, Al-Mizan holds that their rulings belong specifically to the Prophet, since the text supplies no evidence that they apply to others.

verses.30:
Al-Mizan notes that the address now shifts directly to the Prophet’s wives, emphasizing their particular responsibilities and clarifying what virtue requires and forbids. A fāḥishatin mubayyinatin is a clear, manifest, grave indecency, such as harming, defaming, or slandering the Prophet.

Their punishment being doubled means precisely two equal shares, as the following verse’s promise of reward “twice” confirms. The commentary therefore rejects explanations that make it a longer or closer burning in Hell, or a threefold punishment. The statement that this is easy for Allah shows that marriage to the Prophet cannot obstruct God’s punishment: true honour arises only through taqwā. That marriage brings a beautiful result with reverence, but desolation and misery with sinfulness.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that yaqnut means being submissive, or submissive and obedient, to Allah and His Messenger, while aʿtadnā means “We have prepared.” Thus, any of the Prophet’s wives who submits and obeys and performs righteous deeds will receive twice the reward and a generous provision, meaning a place in Paradise.

The shift from the preceding verse’s third-person statement, “this is easy for Allah,” to “We shall reward” and “We have prepared” conveys nearness and honour, in contrast with the desolation and misery conveyed by the doubled punishment.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan holds that the Prophet’s wives are distinguished from other women only conditionally: if they are reverent, they have a higher standing. Their connection to the Prophet does not itself confer that rank. Because of their position, the commands introduced as consequences of their status—avoiding alluring speech, remaining in their homes, not displaying themselves, establishing prayer, giving charity, and obeying Allah and His Messenger—are especially binding upon them, even though such qualities are also desirable for other women. Their individual double punishment and double reward reinforce this heightened responsibility.

They must not speak pleasantly or softly to men in a manner that arouses suspicion or stirs the desire of one whose heart is diseased, namely one lacking the faculty of faith that restrains inclination to ugly acts. Rather, qawlan maʿrūfan is ordinary, straightforward speech: neither melodious nor suggestive, neither hinting at impropriety nor provoking suspicion, but speech approved by Islamic law and custom. Qar­na means remaining or being firmly fixed in their homes. Tabarruj is displaying oneself before people. The first Age of Ignorance, al-jāhiliyyah al-ūlā, denotes the customs prevailing before the Prophet’s first revelation; the alternative historical periods proposed by some exegetes have no evidence. Prayer is singled out as a foundational act of worship, and charity as a foundational act of social interchange; obedience to Allah and His Messenger includes all religious duties and obedience to the Prophet’s commands and prohibitions.

The commentary further argues that innamā in the purification clause restricts God’s will to removing impurity and purification, and restricts these acts to the addressed Ahl al-Bayt. The masculine-inclusive plural ʿankum, rather than the feminine plural ʿankunna used for the wives, proves that the phrase cannot refer specifically to the wives. It must either include them with males or address a different group containing at least one male.

Al-Mizan rejects the suggestions that Ahl al-Bayt means the people of the Sacred House, the people of the Prophet’s Mosque, his household in the customary sense including wives and kin, the Prophet and his wives, or certain kin apart from the wives. It also rejects construing purification as merely the strict piety and observance of religious duties required of the wives. Such piety is required of all Muslims and cannot be the special meaning of a statement confined to the Ahl al-Bayt; nor can the clause be an extension of the wives’ special duties, since others do not share their doubled punishment and reward. Nor can it address only the Prophet and his wives: the Prophet already possesses ʿiṣmah, a divine gift rather than something earned by works, so warning him with punishment or motivating him with reward to acquire taqwā would be senseless. Conversely, interpreting the clause as an unconditional cleansing of the Prophet’s general household or kin conflicts with the fact that the wives’ honour depends on taqwā, whether God’s will is taken as legislative or creational.

The commentary says these difficulties reinforce more than seventy narrations, transmitted through nearly forty Sunni and over thirty Shiʿi chains, which identify the Ahl al-Bayt exclusively as the Prophet, ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, Ḥasan, and Ḥusayn. Although there are more Sunni than Shiʿi reports, both bodies of narration support this identification. Reports from Um Salamah, in whose house the verse was revealed, explicitly exclude the Prophet’s wives, and some are graded authentic (ṣaḥīḥ). Thus, the reports do not merely name ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, Ḥasan, and Ḥusayn without excluding others; many expressly confine the designation to them.

In reply to the objection that the surrounding address to the wives requires their inclusion, Al-Mizan argues that the question is whether the purification sentence was revealed with that address. The reports portray the sentence as revealed separately; none of the more than seventy reports says that it was revealed as the conclusion of the address to the wives, including reports associated with those who identify Ahl al-Bayt with the wives. Its insertion interrupts feminine-plural commands addressed to the wives before and after it, and its import is loftier than those commands. It was therefore either placed there by the Prophet’s command or during the Qur’an’s compilation after his death. In this Qur’anic usage, Ahl al-Bayt is consequently a technical designation limited to the five, not a term extendable even to the Prophet’s nearest kin by customary usage.

Rijs means filth or impurity, physical or metaphorical. Here it is spiritual impurity: the inward pollution arising from false beliefs or from vile deeds. Since al-rijs is general, the verse concerns the removal of every kind of impurity that could divert a person from true belief and right action. This entails divinely granted ʿiṣmah, a mental faculty protecting one from false beliefs and ugly deeds. The emphatic purification removes the effects of impurity and equips a person to recognize truth in belief and action. Accordingly, Allah’s will here is not a legislative command or obligation, but God’s continuous creational will to single out the Ahl al-Bayt for protection from error and sin; through it they are maʿṣūm.

verses.34:
Al-Mizan takes “remember” to mean the opposite of forgetting. This begins a second exhortation to the Prophet’s wives, after the preceding commands setting out their duties: they must keep present in mind the verses of Allah and wisdom recited in their homes, lest they lapse from the path prescribed for them. The mention of their homes adds emphasis.

The commentary rejects the interpretation that the verse merely tells them to be grateful for living where the Qur’an and Sunnah are recited, judging it remote from the wording, especially in light of the conclusion, “Allah has always been subtle, aware.”
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse confirms the equal honour of men and women in Islam: forgiveness and a great recompense are prepared alike for men and women who possess the named virtues. The indefinite form of both forgiveness and recompense signifies their vastness.

The distinction between submitting Muslims and faithful believers shows that islām is outward submission to religion through performing its principal commands, whereas īmān is an inward attachment to and surrender to religion that then motivates one’s deeds. A muslim or muslimah performs that outward submission; a muʾmin or muʾminah cherishes the religion in the heart in a way that inspires action. Every faithful person is Muslim, but not every Muslim is faithful.

Qunūt is submissive obedience. Truthfulness means that a person’s claims, speech, promises, and outward presentation agree with reality. Patience includes endurance in trials, perseverance in religious obligations, and restraint from sin. Khushūʿ is inward humility of the heart, unlike khuḍūʿ, its outward expression through the limbs. Ṣadaqah is spending wealth in God’s way and includes obligatory zakāt; fasting includes both obligatory and recommended fasts. Guarding the private parts means withholding them from those unlawful to one. Abundant remembrance of Allah includes remembrance by the tongue and while lying on one’s side, as well as ritual prayer and the hajj.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains that “decree” concerns binding religious direction, not God’s metaphysical decree of fate. God’s decree establishes religious rulings for His servants through a prophet; the Prophet’s decree concerns governing and managing the community through authority God has granted him. Since the verse joins Allah and His Messenger in decreeing, it particularly concerns such governance, for divine legislation (shariah) belongs solely to God, while the Prophet acts by His authority.

No believing man or woman may regard what Allah and His Messenger decree concerning them as a personal matter over which they retain a choice; they must obey. The plural in lahum al-khīrah min amrihim includes all believers and suggests that they regard the decreed matters as their own separate affairs, whereas amran, singular, denotes God’s single decree.

The commentary treats this as a general principle, though it is possible, in light of what follows, that it prepares for 33:40 by alluding to objections over the Prophet’s marriage to Zayd’s former wife because Zayd had been his adopted son.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan identifies the man favoured by Allah and by the Prophet as Zayd ibn Ḥārithah, whom Allah guided to faith and endeared to the Prophet, and whom the Prophet treated kindly, freed, and adopted. Zayd was married to Zaynab bint Jaḥsh, the Prophet’s paternal cousin. When Zayd wished to divorce her, the Prophet told him, “Hold fast to your wife, and be mindful of Allah,” meaning that he should not divorce her, though the wording indicates Zayd’s insistence. Zayd nevertheless divorced her, and the Prophet married her.

What the Prophet concealed was what Allah would disclose. His fear of people was not personal or blameworthy: he feared that public reproach and the aspersions of sick-hearted people would harm the faith of the masses and thus his prophetic mission. This was fear for God’s sake and, in that respect, fear of God. Yet the verse gently reproves him, directing him to fear God alone and not to withhold what God would make manifest. God had ordained his marriage to Zaynab and secured him against criticism; the wording, “We wedded her to you” and “Allah’s command is always carried out,” shows that this marriage was not the Prophet’s personal choice but the execution of God’s command.

“Zayd had no further want of her” (qaḍā… waṭaran) politely states that Zayd’s marriage had been consummated. The marriage’s purpose was to remove difficulty for believers in marrying the former wives of adopted sons once those sons had no further want of them, even after consummation; this differs from the former wife of a biological son, whom one may not marry. The verse therefore shows that what the Prophet hid was God’s decree that he marry Zaynab, not personal desire or passionate love for a married woman. Al-Mizan rejects the latter claim: his divine training should overcome such instinct, and, if the matter were merely such desire, there would be no reason to reproach him for concealing it, since Islam forbids eyeing another man’s wife.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains that faraḍa means what Allah has stipulated or assigned, and may also mean what He has allowed; ḥaraj means discomfort or difficulty. Thus, nothing can obstruct or make burdensome the Prophet’s doing what God commands or permits for him.

This is Allah’s established sunnah with the preceding prophets and messengers. Allah determines for every individual what suits that person. Prophets are permitted what others are permitted, except for the particular permissions and prohibitions that apply to the Prophet.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan takes “those” to elaborate on the earlier reference to those who came before: the prophets and messengers who convey Allah’s messages. Khashiyah is an inward state of fearing an unwanted thing or its cause. The prophets have khashiyah only of God because they know that He alone controls the universe.

Khashiyah differs from khawf, which is an outward, practical unease that leads one to guard against a threat, whether or not fear enters the heart. Prophets may have khawf of people, as in Moses’ flight and the Prophet’s fear of a people’s treachery, although the two terms are sometimes used synonymously. Hence prophets do not have khashiyah of anyone but God. If the context suggests hesitation in delivering the message, concern that something may hinder its delivery belongs to their conveying of the message, since all their deeds and words are part of it. Allah is ḥasīban, accounting for every small and great deed; therefore He alone must be feared.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse answers objections to the Prophet’s marriage to the former wife of his adopted son. Muḥammad was neither Zayd’s biological father nor the father of any adult men then living; “men” refers to grown males alive when the verse was revealed. The statement is not a command that he not father sons, but an expression that God had decreed that none of his male children would survive to manhood. Thus marrying Zayd’s divorced wife was not like marrying the former wife of a biological son: adoption and calling someone a son do not give him a biological son’s legal status.

Al-Qāsim, al-Ṭayyib, al-Ṭāhir, and Ibrāhim were the Prophet’s biological sons, but died before manhood. Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn were his grandsons, and he died before they reached manhood. None therefore contradicts the verse.

A khātam is a seal or a thing that imprints one. By calling Muḥammad the seal of the prophets, the verse declares that prophethood ends with him and that there is no prophet after him. A rasūl delivers God’s message to people, while a nabī conveys news of the unseen concerning religion and its truths; since a messenger must be a prophet, the end of prophethood also ends messengership. Muḥammad is therefore the seal of both prophets and messengers. Mentioning this also recalls that his relation to the people is that of God’s messenger and prophet, so what he does is by God’s command. “Allah knows all things” means that what He has disclosed was already within His knowledge.
verses.41: Al-Mizan explains that dhikr, the opposite of forgetting, is directing one’s attention to what is remembered. Uttering God’s names and attributes is one form of dhikr, not its whole meaning.
verses.42: Al-Mizan explains that tasbīḥ is to declare God free of every imperfection, and is not confined to verbally saying subḥān Allāh. Bukratan is the day’s beginning and aṣīlan its end after the afternoon. These transitional times especially call for glorification of the eternally subsisting God, who is above the change that affects day and night; they may also figuratively mean all times.
verses.43: Al-Mizan explains that yuṣallī, from ṣalāt and broadly denoting inclination toward someone, means here God’s particular mercy toward the faithful, which brings eternal happiness. Exegetes distinguish God’s ṣalāt as mercy, the angels’ as seeking forgiveness, and other people’s as duʿāʾ. God’s ṣalāt is His merciful remembrance of the believers: when they remember and glorify Him abundantly, He remembers them abundantly, surrounds them with light, and removes them from darkness. Thus the verse follows the command to remember God as cause and effect. Darkness is forgetfulness and heedlessness of God, while light is remembrance of Him. By saying that He is merciful “towards the faithful,” the verse emphasizes that faith is what calls forth this mercy.
verses.44: Al-Mizan explains that “their greeting” is passive in sense: on the day they meet God, the angels and their Lord will greet them with peace. They will therefore have complete safety and security, untouched by vexation or punishment, along with the generous recompense God has prepared for them.
verses.45: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is a witness because he witnesses the deeds of people—or the ummah—in this world and reports them on the Day of Resurrection. As bearer of glad tidings, he promises divine reward and Paradise to the faithful who obey God and His Messenger; as warner, he warns the faithless and disobedient of punishment and the Fire.
verses.46: Al-Mizan explains that calling to Allah is calling people to faith in God alone, which necessarily includes faith in His religion. “By His permission” refers to the Prophet’s formal appointment to prophethood. The lamp spreading light metaphorically describes his guidance to true happiness and rescue from the darkness of misery and misguidance. The view that the shining light refers to the Qur’an is considered remote from the wording.
verses.47: Al-Mizan explains that faḍl is what one receives beyond what one has earned or deserved. Divine reward is therefore not merely proportionate to a deed, but grace exceeding it; the verse does not limit this grace to the Hereafter.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains that not heeding their annoyances means turning away from what troubles the Prophet and not concerning himself with it. Trust in Allah means that he should not repel their intrusions alone, but take God as his protector, for God suffices as a protector.
verses.49: Al-Mizan explains that nakaḥtum means concluding the marriage contract, while tamassūhunna euphemistically means consummation. A woman divorced after the contract but before consummation has no waiting-period (ʿiddah); she must receive a settlement suited to her circumstances and social standing and be divorced without animosity. This applies whether or not a mahr was specified: where it was specified, the related ruling requires half the agreed dowry (2:237), and where it was not, this verse still requires that she be given something.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan identifies seven categories made lawful to the Prophet: wives given their dowries, female war captives in his possession, daughters of his paternal uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles, and maternal aunts who fled with him, and a believing woman who gives herself to him. Ujūr means muhūr, or dowries. The descriptions concerning prior payment of dowry and capture in war further explain these categories rather than restrict them. Some exegetes take the paternal relatives to denote Quraysh women and the maternal relatives to denote Banū Zuhrah women. Majmaʿ al-Bayān reports that the migration condition belonged to a period when the Prophet could not marry non-migrant women, though this was later permitted.

A believing woman who gives herself to the Prophet is a Muslim woman content to marry him without ṣidāq or mahr, should he wish to marry her. This concession belongs to him alone, not to other believers; the statement that God knows what He ordained for them regarding wives and those their right hands possess further stresses the Prophet’s special rulings. “So that there may be no difficulty for you” most likely explains the initial grant of lawfulness, though it could less likely explain why the latter strictures are exclusive to him. The verse closes by invoking God’s forgiveness and mercy.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains turjī as putting off, here politely meaning rejecting, and tuʾwī as lodging, here figuratively meaning accepting and drawing a woman to oneself. In context, the Prophet may accept or reject a woman who offers herself to him; if he later seeks one initially rejected, he incurs no blame, since he may either accept or reject her.

The verse may also mean that he may apportion his time among his wives as he wishes, rather than observe a fixed nightly rotation: he may advance or delay a wife’s turn, remain apart from her for a time, and later return to her. This interpretation better suits the assurance that they will be comforted rather than grieve: an advanced turn brings happiness, while a delayed turn leaves hope. God knows what benefits His servants and does not hasten punishment. Al-Mizan holds that these interpretations best fit the surrounding context and narrations from Ahl al-Bayt, unlike other exegetical proposals.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan gives three possible readings of the prohibition on the Prophet taking women afterwards. Read independently, it bars marriage to anyone beyond the wives who chose to remain with him rather than divorce; the ban on replacing wives reinforces this. Read with the preceding passage beginning “We have made lawful to you…,” it bars marriage outside the six specified groups, since those whom his right hand possesses remain excepted. Narrations from the Imāms instead indicate that it concerns the women forbidden in Qur’an 4:23 (Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters…). Thus “afterwards” may mean after the nine wives remained with him, outside the groups of 33:50, or outside those forbidden for marriage in 4:23.

“Nor exchange them for other wives” means divorcing one or more wives in order to marry replacements, while “except for what your right hand possesses” excepts slave-girls from the prohibition. God’s watching over all things also conveys a veiled threat.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan presents this as etiquette for visitors to the Prophet’s homes. They may enter only by invitation for a meal, not arrive early and wait for the food to cook, nor linger after eating in order to hear private conversation. Both waiting for the food and lingering to listen are prohibited because they vex the Prophet, though his modesty keeps him from asking people to leave; God declares the truth about the proper etiquette.

When people need something from the Prophet’s wives, they must ask from behind a curtain, a rule said to purify both parties’ hearts. It is also forbidden to trouble the Messenger by violating these commands or others concerning his wives, and no one may ever marry his wives after him; such a marriage is an enormity before God. The verse suggests that some had already hinted that they would marry them after his death, as narrations also report.
verses.54: Al-Mizan takes God’s knowledge of deeds done openly or secretly as a threat to those who vexed the Prophet or boasted that they would marry his wives after him.
verses.55: Al-Mizan explains that the pronoun refers to the Prophet’s wives and exempts their fathers, sons, brothers, nephews, and other maḥrams from the requirement to consult them from behind a curtain. Some exegetes say paternal and maternal uncles are omitted because they might describe the wives to their sons. “Their women” means believing women alone, excluding kāfir women, while those whom their right hands possess includes both male and female slaves. The command to be mindful of God, who witnesses all things, reinforces the ruling, especially through its shift from speaking about the wives to addressing them directly.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains yuṣallūn, from ṣalāt, as having the basic sense of inclining or bowing. God’s ṣalāt upon the Prophet is His unconditional merciful inclination toward him; the angels’ ṣalāt purifies him and seeks his forgiveness; and the faithful’s ṣalāt is their prayer that God’s mercy encompass him. God’s and the angels’ ṣalāt precede that of the faithful because the latter depends on them and cannot come before them. Many Shiʿi and Sunni narrations state that ṣalāt upon the Prophet is performed by asking God to bless him and his family.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan maintains that no one can truly annoy God, who is above irritation or any defect in divinity. Describing both God and His Messenger as annoyed honors the Prophet: to wish ill to the Messenger, who is his Lord’s messenger, is also to wish ill to God.

God’s curse means remoteness from His mercy. Since that mercy for the faithful consists in guidance to true beliefs and faith that produce righteous deeds, being cursed in this world means deprivation of such guidance through one’s misconduct, akin to the hardening and sealing of the heart. In the hereafter it means exclusion from the mercy of nearness to God, being veiled from Him. The promised punishment is humiliating because those who arrogantly antagonized God and His Messenger in this world will be debased in the next.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains that “undeservedly” excludes discomfort imposed with just cause, such as qiṣāṣ, ḥadd, or a judge’s discretionary punishment (taʿdhīr). But one who harasses faithful men or women without cause bears defamation and a glaring sin. Buhtān is a false accusation made against someone to their face, rather than secret gossip. Such harassment resembles it because the harasser confronts the faithful with accusations that treat their alleged conduct as blameworthy when it is not. It is a glaring sin because defamation is intrinsically known by the intellect to be wrong, without needing a ruling of shariah.
verses.59: Al-Mizan explains jalābībihinna as cloaks that envelop the whole body, or as a khimār covering the head and face. Letting them down means covering oneself so that the chest and bosom are concealed from view. Such covering makes women more likely to be recognized as “people of covering and righteousness” (ahl al-sitr wa al-ṣalāḥ) and thus not harassed by hypocrites. Although some exegetes interpret recognition as identification as free Muslim women rather than slave-girls or non-Muslims, Al-Mizan holds that the first interpretation fits better.
verses.60: Al-Mizan explains yantahī as ceasing and murjafūn as people who spread false slander to upset others or incite unrest; la-nughriyannaka means that God will spur the Prophet against them. If hypocrites, sick-hearted people, and those spreading false rumours in the city to provoke unrest among Muslims do not cease their sedition, they will be driven out. They will remain the Prophet’s neighbours only briefly: the interval between the edict of banishment and its execution.
verses.61: Al-Mizan explains thuqifū, the passive of thaqafa, as being found out and captured. The clause describes the hypocrites, sick-hearted people, and agitators as cursed: wherever they are found, they are seized and slain.
verses.62: Al-Mizan explains sunnah as a path usually or always trodden. God’s threatened exile and execution of hypocrites, insurgents, and agitators follows His unchanging way with earlier peoples: whenever people worked corruption, incited civil unrest, or became lawless or tyrannical, He seized them. The same way will be enacted among this community.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains that the question about the Hour concerns when it will occur, whether near or distant. God commands the Prophet to declare that its knowledge belongs to Allah alone. The statement that it may be near emphasizes its unknowability and shows that the Prophet does not know its time any more than other people do, rather than concealing a revelation about it.
verses.64: Al-Mizan explains that Allah’s cursing of the deniers (kuffār) means distancing them from His mercy. He has prepared (aʿadda) for them saʿīr, a kindled and blazing fire.
verses.65: Al-Mizan distinguishes a walī from a naṣīr: a walī takes complete charge of a matter, with the mawlā ceding it to him, whereas a naṣīr gives assistance in only some aspects while the person assisted remains involved. Thus the deniers will find neither one to take their affair wholly in hand nor one to help them partially.
verses.66: Al-Mizan explains that the faces of those in the Fire will either change in appearance—becoming yellow, black, or gloomy—or be turned over so as to receive the Fire more fully, like meat being grilled. Their wish that they had obeyed Allah and the Messenger is an expression of regret and futile hope.
verses.67: Al-Mizan explains that sādatanā is the plural of sayyid: lords, rulers, chiefs, or nobles responsible for a large group. Kubarāʾ is the plural of kabīr, and may here mean elders, since people ordinarily follow their chiefs or elders.
verses.68: Al-Mizan explains that ḍiʿfayn means two identical shares. The followers ask that their leaders receive double punishment because those leaders led both themselves and others astray; for the same reason, they ask that God curse them heavily.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as forbidding believers to treat the Prophet as some Israelites treated Moses: by troubling or slandering him. “Vexed” is not confined to injury in speech or deed, though both are forbidden; Allah’s absolving Moses indicates that the Israelites had defamed him. The verse’s silence about the precise charge possibly supports narrations that they alleged a deficiency in Moses’s male organ, from which God cleared him.

Regarding those who troubled the Prophet, the commentary considers the incident of Zayd and Zaynab the most likely referent. Even so, many narrations concerning that story must be rejected because they conflict with the Prophet’s sanctity and holiness. Moses’s being absolved, together with his lofty position before Allah and the succeeding verse, can be understood as a prohibition against troubling the Prophet.
verses.70: Al-Mizan explains sadīdan as speaking correctly and rightly: truthfully and purposefully, rather than in gossip or slander. Believers must verify the truth of what they say and ensure that their speech is neither vain nor harmful.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains that the rectification of deeds and forgiveness of sins follow from speaking rightly. One who has acquired truthful, purposeful speech abandons lying, vain and harmful speech; this necessarily removes vulgar, depraved, abhorrent, and useless conduct as well. His deeds are therefore rectified, and regret for a sinful past is sufficient for repentance.

For the rest of his life, God will preserve such a person from danger; if he commits lesser sins, God will forgive them, as stated: If you avoid the greater acts that you have been forbidden, We shall absolve you of the lesser ones (4:31). Thus, by God’s permission, right speech reforms conduct and brings forgiveness. The great victory promised to one who obeys Allah and His Messenger is the future reward resulting from righteous deeds and avoidance of what is forbidden. This effectively concludes the sūrah’s central theme of obedience underlying its duties and prohibitions, while the final two verses supplement this meaning.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains amānah as something entrusted to a person for safekeeping and eventual return to its depositor. Since the consequences of this trust divide its bearers into hypocrites, mushriks, and believers, it undoubtedly pertains to the true religion (al-dīn al-ḥaqq). The commentary rejects identifying it with correct belief in God’s oneness, because the heavens, earth, and all things already glorify God—“There is no thing that does not glorify Allah (17:44)”—whereas they declined this trust. It also rejects mere acceptance of religious beliefs and acts, or the scrupulous performance of prescribed acts, because every human being undertook the trust although most do not accept or know the true faith. Nor can it be a perfection reached merely through belief in divine unity or acceptance of religion: all humanity bears it, and eternal felicity or misery follows from deeds issuing from belief, not belief alone.

The commentary concludes that the trust is divine wilāyah (al-wilāyah al-ilāhiyyah): the perfection attained through true beliefs, righteous action, and ascent from materiality to sincere faith in God alone. Through complete sincerity and submission, without associating anything with God, a human being cedes the management of his affairs to God, who becomes his walī, complete guardian and authority. The offering of this trust to the heavens, earth, mountains, and humanity is figurative: it measures their inherent ability to bear it, and their acceptance or refusal likewise signifies possessing or lacking that capacity. Despite their vastness and strength, the heavens, earth, and mountains cannot bear it, so they fear it and refuse it. Humanity, though small and weak, has the requisite capacity and accepts its severe weight. Human beings are consequently divided, according to their faithfulness to the trust, into hypocrites, mushriks, and believers; unlike them, the heavens, earth, and mountains are all obedient and faithful.

Al-Mizan addresses the objection that it would be unwise for God to impose such a perilous burden on an unjust and foolish being, particularly when the mighty heavens, earth, and mountains refused it. The reply is that, although injustice and ignorance are normally blameworthy, a being capable of being unjust can also become just, and one capable of ignorance can become learned. The heavens, earth, and mountains can be called neither unjust and ignorant nor just and learned. Humanity’s capacity for injustice and ignorance is therefore what enables it to bear the trust and develop knowledge and justice. Divine wilāyah and perfected servitude arise from knowing God and acting rightly, and are described through knowledge and justice precisely because their bearer can lack them. Thus, although humanity is initially unjust toward itself and ignorant of the grave consequence of betraying the burden—eternal perdition—it can rise from injustice and ignorance to justice and knowledge. The descriptions ẓalūm and jahūl indicate this capacity, whether understood as character descriptions or intensified forms.

The phrase “So Allah will punish” may express the final outcome of bearing the trust: punishment of male and female hypocrites and mushriks. A person who betrays the trust while concealing that betrayal is a hypocrite, which may explain why hypocrites are mentioned before mushriks. Joined to this is the other outcome: Allah turns mercifully toward male and female believers. If they have faith and have not betrayed the trust, He manages their affairs as their walī, guides them toward Himself, conceals their injustice and ignorance, and adorns them with beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds; He is forgiving and merciful. The shift from first person to third person in “So Allah will punish” shows that the final end of all matters belongs to God, and the explicit repetition of Allah in “Allah will turn” emphasizes His concern for believers’ rights and affairs.

The commentary accepts that religious duties (taklīf) can be called the trust in the sense that offering, refusal, and acceptance would still refer figuratively to capacity for them. Yet duties are prerequisites for attaining divine wilāyah and perfecting servitude, not the ultimate goal itself. Other exegetes have identified the trust as religious obligations that lead to Paradise or the Fire, the intellect underlying those obligations, the phrase lā ilāha illā Allāh, the bodily organs entrusted for proper use, deposited trusts and promises, or knowledge of God and its implications; the last comes nearest to the commentary’s meaning. They have also construed the offering literally, whether to inhabitants of the heavens such as angels, or to heavens, earth, and mountains endowed with understanding and presented with reward and punishment; as the trust’s figurative contest with those creations; or as a hypothetical presentation of duties to them if they were granted understanding. Al-Mizan holds that the preceding analysis exposes the weaknesses of these views.
